Issued at 249 PM CDT Mon Sep 7 2026

Partly to mostly cloudy skies are occurring early this afternoon 
across the region ahead of an approaching 500mb trough. Ongoing 
southerly flow is expected to provide deep moisture advection into 
the CWA this evening into tonight, with IVT showing moisture coming 
both from the Gulf and some moisture from Tropical Storm Marie 
offshore from Baja California. The 12z sounding from KINL revealed 
an already moist PWAT of 1.47", which is above the 90th percentile 
of 1.14". As moisture advection occurs tonight, these PWAT values 
are progged to increase up to around 2", which would be towards, if 
not breaking, the max of climatology. 

This surge of moisture, combined with a deep warm cloud layer in 
excess of 12,000 ft, will likely lead to localized very heavy 
rainfall rates this evening through tonight. Flash flooding concerns 
are somewhat mitigated due to drier soil moisture conditions across 
a large portion of the CWA, although areas north of the Laurentian 
Divide show soil moistures in the 50-60% range per MRMS CREST soil 
moisture. That being said, there is still a minor concern for flash 
flooding tonight, including the northwest Wisconsin portion of the 
CWA, as very heavy rainfall occurring over the areas experiencing 
Extreme (D3) drought could potentially lead to rapid runoff. 

In terms of QPF, heaviest rainfall is expected to be overnight as a 
quasi-stationary warm front remains parked north of the CWA and a 
cold front approaches from the west. 24-hour LPMM QPF forecasts from 
the 12z HREF suggest the potential for 2-3" of precip occurring from 
multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms moving through tonight 
into early Tuesday morning. Confidence in the area of heaviest QPF 
is fairly low, although it does appear more likely along and south 
of US-2, where PWATs will be higher. Storm motion will be relatively 
progressive tonight, which limits flood concerns, although training 
storms will be something to monitor tonight into tomorrow morning. 

Besides potential flash flood concerns, there is also a Marginal 
Risk for severe thunderstorms today through tonight for portions of 
north-central MN around the Brainerd Lakes. MUCAPE per the RAP is 
forecast to increase in excess of 1000-1500 J/kg overnight, with a 
stout 850mb LLJ of 30-40 knots and 0-6 km bulk shear of 40-50 knots. 
These overnight storms will most likely be elevated, with large hail 
and damaging winds being potential hazards. Confidence in severe 
storms tonight is low, as CAMs show somewhat weak mid-level lapse 
rates and the warm nose associated with the LLJ will likely keep 
storms decoupled from the surface. 

A Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms persist on Tuesday morning 
in the Arrowhead, I-35 corridor, and northwest Wisconsin. However, 
this threat of severe storms will most likely be remnants of the 
convection tonight as the cold front sweeps through and will 
therefore share similar limitations to severe hazards as previously 
mentioned. Expect showers and thunderstorms to largely come to an 
end across the CWA by Noon on Tuesday. Sprinkles and the occasional 
shower may linger through the afternoon as the sfc cold front 
continues to move through. 

Following the cold frontal passage on Tuesday, a more benign pattern 
settles over the CWA around mid-week as high pressure builds. Ahead 
of this high pressure, west-northwest winds are very likely to 
become strong during the daytime hours on Wednesday. Wind gusts of 
30-40 mph are forecast, strongest in the Arrowhead. A few gusts in 
excess of 40 mph are not totally out of the question, although the 
NBM probability for inland locations along the North Shore is a low 
10-20%. Wind Advisories may be needed on Wednesday, especially if 
winds show an increasing trend. 

The next chance for precipitation arrives late into the week into 
the weekend as additional troughs potentially propagate through the 
CWA. One upcoming pattern change of note is a temperature change 
arriving this weekend into early next week. While high temps most of 
this workweek will be in the 70s for most, high temps by this 
weekend into early next week will likely be in the 60s (with a few 
upper 50s not out of the question!).
